newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan CPC eyes price hike to restore profits.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan CPC eyes price hike to restore profits.

text.p: Taiwan monopoly Chinese Petroleum said on Tuesday it would seek state permission to raise petrol prices five to eight percent to shore up its badly sagging bottom line.

The company, whose fiscal 1997 budget is still stalled in parliament four months into the new fiscal year, is free to raise prices by only three percent or less a month, and must seek government approval for anything bigger.
"Chinese Petroleum will ask for the Ministry of Economics' approval for a five to eight percent gasoline price hike to help the poor profit," company spokesman Fang Yi-shan told Reuters.

Chinese Petroleum reported on Tuesday that its pre-tax profits in the first three months of fiscal year 1997 beginning on July 1 were T$1.201 billion (US$43.6 million), well short of a budgeted T$4.629 billion (US$168 million).
Company executives blamed high oil import costs for the profit gap, saying prevailing international crude prices were much higher than the company had budgeted for.
The average crude import prices for the first three months were US$18.18, US$18.63 and US$19.45 per barrel, much higher than the state firm's budgeted US$15.26, an official said.
For each increase of 50 Taiwan cents in the retail price of petrol, Chinese Petroleum enjoys a jump of T$300-400 million (US$11-14.5 million) in its monthly pre-tax profits, Fang said.
Its 95-octane petrol now sells for T$16.5 per litre (US$2.27 per gallon) at Taiwan's filling stations.
Fang said that because Chinese Petroleum's fiscal 1997 budget was stalled in an obligatory parliamentary review, the Economics Ministry might not be able to approve the price hike.
"It is difficult to adjust price before legislators agree on our budget," Fang said.
